Verdict: the mathematics holds, but one sentence of the statement is false as written, so I set holds=false. Everything else is confirmed: the three formulas, the transferred bounds, their sharpness and attainment, and the example values. The needed corrections are small; they are in corrected_statement.

My own proof of the rates underlying S1/S2 (unit sphere; general R follows by scaling). Write x_i = c + xi_i, with c = cos(beta) n and xi_i perpendicular to n, |xi_i| = sin(beta).
- The cross product splits as x_j x x_i = cos(beta) n x (xi_i - xi_j) + xi_j x xi_i. So the sphere velocity is v_i = cos(beta) u_i + nu_i n. Here u_i is the planar Biot-Savart velocity of the chord triangle, and nu_i = -u_i . xi_i.
- For a zero-impulse shape with sum Gamma_i Gamma_j = 0, the center of vorticity zeta lies on the circumcircle, and u_i = alpha w_i + b n x w_i with w_i = xi_i - zeta.
- By direct expansion, v_i = s w_i + Omega x w_i, with s = cos(beta) alpha and Omega = cos(beta) b n + rho (b a - alpha n x a), where a = zeta/rho. So the three vortices and p move by an exact 3D similarity about p.
- The pole therefore obeys ndot = Omega x n. This gives d cos(beta)/dt = -rho^2 alpha = -K a and psidot = [Omega.p - (Omega.n) cos(beta)]/sin^2(beta) = b/rho^2, the planar Im kappa with no cos(beta) factor. Here a = Re(kappa) r^2 and b = Im(kappa) r^2 depend only on the shape.
- Measures (1)-(3) follow in a few lines: (1) = |b|/(2|a| cos(beta)); (2) uses t_c - t = (1 - cos(beta))/(K|a|); (3) uses dpsi/d ln tan^2(beta/2) = b/(2a).
- Transfer of the bound: collapse forces the conserved quantity sum Gamma_i Gamma_j l_ij^2 = R^2 (sum Gamma)^2 - |M|^2 to be zero, and conservation of H forces sum Gamma_i Gamma_j = 0. The chord ODE is the planar ODE times cos(beta). So the chord shape is a planar collapsing shape, which is realizable at every beta with either sign of d. Hence P0 >= P_-(mu) > sqrt3/2 by the paper's Theorem 1.

Numerical checks (my own code, my own shape parametrization z3 = mu/(1+mu) + r e^{i theta}):
- static_check.py: 50 digits, 2001 configurations. These cover 9 values of mu (including mu > 1), random theta on both arcs, beta in {1e-6, (0.01, 1.5), pi/2 +/- 1e-3, (1.65, 3.1), pi - 1e-5}, R in {1, 2.37, 0.41}, plus 60 random unnormalized circulation triples with sum Gamma_i Gamma_j = 0.
- Worst residuals: tangency 2e-45; dM/dt 9e-51; |p| - R 2e-50; spread of the log-chord rates (vortex pairs and vortex-to-p) 8e-39; 3D similarity fit 2e-44; d cos(beta)/dt + K a 7e-35; psidot vs b/rho^2 1e-38; (1) vs P0 |sec beta| 1e-38; (2) vs P0 sec^2(beta/2) 5e-37; (3) vs P0 7e-35.
- The smallest P0 sampled was 0.9649, above sqrt3/2.
- dyn_check.py integrates the ODE with DOP853 (rtol 1e-13). Six whole burst -> great circle -> collapse runs, with beta0 between 2.5 and 3.1 and integration down to beta of about 0.02, for mu = 0.05 to 2 and R = 0.6 to 2.
- Results: the linear law for cos(beta) holds to 3e-10; t_c from a fit to the integrated data matches the formula to 6e-11; chords stay proportional to sin(beta) to 2e-8; the loxodrome law psi(beta) holds to 5e-6 absolute on windings of order 100, and to 1e-9 for moderate P0; measures (1) and (2) along the trajectories hold to 9e-7.
- planar_floor.py (40 digits): P_-(1/2) = 1.06470597627120434, P_+(1/2) = 2.20385501603613279, P_-(1) = sqrt2. P_-(mu) - sqrt3/2 is about 1.3 mu^2, and P_-(mu) increases on the tested grid down to mu = 1e-8.
- The beta = 30 degree floors are exactly 1 and 4 sqrt3 - 6 = 0.9282032...

Defects found:
- (a) The statement says the chord shapes are exactly the planar zero-impulse shapes excluding the collinear ones. The equilateral triangle is also a zero-impulse shape; the paper itself calls theta = +/-theta0 zero-impulse relative equilibria. edge_check.py confirms that on the sphere the equilateral chord triangle has d l^2/dt ~ 1e-51 while the vortices move at speed about 0.1-0.5. So it is a relative equilibrium, never a collapse, and it must be excluded too. This does not affect the bounds, since the equilateral shape is not a collapse and has P = infinity.
- (b) At the great-circle instant beta = pi/2, measure (1) is undefined and both sides of the bound are infinite. So "at every instant" should exclude that instant.
- (c) psi and omega are not defined in the statement. They must be the azimuth of the circumcircle pole about p, with the pole oriented so that collapse is at beta -> 0. Individual vortex azimuths about p rotate at different rates at finite size, which matches the ledger note on Kidambi-Newton. For example, at mu = 0.01 and beta = 0.8 the pole winding is 1.2432 and the vortex windings are 1.2432, 1.504 and 1.503. The per-vortex windings I sampled nevertheless stayed above the floor.

Novelty: I did no new literature search. The ledger records the Kidambi-Newton chord equations and the fact that the sphere has no single omega t_c, so the choice of the pole azimuth is what makes these measures well defined.

No source I could find states any spherical winding measure or any lower bound on one. Several sources state the ingredients.

1. Borisov and Lebedev 1998, RCD 3(4), arXiv nlin/0503057. I read the collapse section in the local extract lit/bl.txt, lines 195-300.
   - On the sphere it gives t = A R^2 (1 - sqrt(1 - B/R^2)) and M_k = D_k R^2 (1 - (1 - t/(A R^2))^2), where M_k are the squared chords. This is the law "1 - cos beta is linear in t" used for t_c - t in measure (2).
   - It also says the vortices scatter from one point, reach the "equator" and then approach "some other point". That is the global picture of point, then great-circle state, then point.
   - It computes no rotation, winding or spiral angle.
   - Side note: "some other point" looks inconsistent with conservation of M = sum Gamma_i x_i. When sum Gamma_i Gamma_j = 0, S^2 = sum Gamma_i^2 > 0, so S is not zero and both ends sit at the same point M/S. S1 has this right.

2. Drivas, Khanikati and Khanikati 2026, arXiv:2607.16490. I read Section 3.1 in lit/s2607.txt.
   - Lemma 3.1 (credited to Kidambi-Newton) gives the collapse conditions on the sphere: L = 0 in chord lengths, and sum of 1/Gamma_i = 0.
   - The collapse is self-similar in chord length but not in geodesic distance.
   - So the claim that chord shapes on the sphere are the planar zero-impulse shapes is known.
   - Nothing on rotation, pitch or bounds.

3. Kidambi and Newton, Nuovo Cimento C 22, 779 (1999).
   - Known from search summaries and the project ledger (RESEARCH.md lines 412, 1054 and 1060; PR #74). The ledger records that the full PDF was read on 2026-09-20.
   - Partner states with two collapse times, depending on the sign of the parallelepiped volume. This is the "either sign of d" placement.
   - The centre-of-vorticity vector must have length R.
   - Each vortex has its own azimuthal velocity, and no omega t_c product is given.
   - Its abstract says the collapse trajectories are projected onto the stereographic plane, where a new Hamiltonian system is derived.
   - I could not reopen it: the host is blocked.

4. Kidambi and Newton, Physica D 116 (1998): collapse conditions (abstract level, via summaries).

5. Krishnamurthy, Aref and Stremler 2018, arXiv:1706.00731. I read the extract lit/kas.txt, lines 904-905: for L = 0, "one point on the circumcircle is always at the center of vorticity". This is the planar fact that becomes "the collapse point lies on the vortices' small circle" on the sphere.

6. Krishnamurthy and Stremler, RCD 2018 (via the project's NOVELTY-AUDIT.md item 4 and internet-search notes).
   - Normalized circumcenter path length s(1) = sqrt(1 + 4P^2), with a numerical observation that s(1) > 2.
   - That is the planar floor P > sqrt3/2, observed numerically only, with no proof and no statement that it is sharp.
   - It is planar only.

7. Search-summary level only, not read: Kimura 1999, Proc. R. Soc. A 455 (unified S^2/H^2 formulation by stereographic projection); Kidambi-Newton 2000, Physica D 140 (streamline topologies, including a collapsing solution); Vankerschaver-Leok arXiv:1211.4560 (numerical collapse test on the sphere); Ohsawa arXiv:2202.01860 (shape dynamics on the sphere); Sakajo 1999, JJIAM. None of their summaries mentions a loxodrome, a rhumb line, a spiral angle, rotation per e-fold, omega (t_c - t), or a winding bound on the sphere.

8. About 16 WebSearch queries in all: loxodrome and rhumb-line variants, "loxodromic" Möbius, stereographic log spiral, Russian-language, Krishnamurthy on the sphere, time-of-collapse and great-circle phrasing. None turned up a spherical winding statement.

result.reasoning:
This result has three parts, and they carry different novelty risk.

(a) Known ingredients, which should not be claimed:
- The shapes that collapse on the sphere are the planar L = 0 chord shapes (Kidambi-Newton 1998; Drivas et al. Lemma 3.1).
- Partner placements with two collapse times (Kidambi-Newton 1999).
- |M| = |S| R.
- The time law, with chord^2 proportional to 1 - (1 - t/T)^2 and a lifetime of 2T. This is in Borisov-Lebedev 1998, so t_c - t = R^2 (1 - cos beta)/A is classical.
- The global picture: vortices leave a point, reach a great circle, then collapse (Borisov-Lebedev).
- The planar fact that the centre of vorticity lies on the circumcircle (Krishnamurthy-Aref-Stremler 2018).

(b) The winding identities (1)-(3). These are the psi(beta) loxodrome law of S2 rewritten in three normalizations: d psi/d ln l^2 = P0 sec beta, and omega (t_c - t) = P0 sec^2(beta/2), which is S2's rate law times the classical time law.
- I found no source that states the loxodrome, the tangent 2P0 against the meridian, or either curvature factor.
- The main residual risk is Kidambi-Newton 1999. It projects the collapse onto the stereographic plane and derives a Hamiltonian system there. S2 says the circle centre's stereographic image is an exact planar log spiral, so that section could contain the psi law, or an equivalent, without the ledger reader noticing: the 2026-09-20 read was hunting for an omega t_c product, not an angle law.
- Secondary risks, all unread: Kimura 1999 (stereographic unification of S^2 and H^2), Newton's 2001 book (chapter 4) and Kidambi-Newton 1998 (full collapse section).
- A write-up should say plainly that omega here is the azimuth rate of the small-circle centre about the collapse point. That is a different observable from the per-vortex azimuthal velocities Kidambi-Newton report as distinct, so it does not contradict them or the ledger's "no single omega t_c".

(c) The sharp floors and their curvature strengthening. I rate these least likely to be in print.
- Any sphere statement would first need the planar floor P > sqrt3/2. That floor appears only as a numerical observation, s(1) > 2, in Krishnamurthy-Stremler 2018. The paper itself leaves priority of its proof unconfirmed.
- None of the sphere literature I reached computes a winding quantity at all.
- Two caveats on significance rather than priority. First, (c) is a corollary: given S1 and S2 and the planar theorem, the transfer is two lines. Second, floor (3) > sqrt3/2 is exactly Krishnamurthy-Stremler's numerical planar observation applied to a spherical quantity that S2 shows equals planar P0. So its only new content is S2's identification plus the planar proof.

Overall: I found no statement of the spherical winding measures or their floors. The label is "probably unstated", not "unclear", because the headline bound requires a planar result that is not proved anywhere I could find.

Conservative wording for any write-up:
- Present (1)-(3) as consequences of the loxodrome law.
- Credit Borisov-Lebedev and Kidambi-Newton for the time law, the partner states and the global picture.
- Credit Krishnamurthy-Stremler for the numerical planar observation.
- Do not claim novelty until Kidambi-Newton 1999's stereographic section, and ideally Kimura 1999, have been re-read specifically for a trajectory angle law.

On the ledger: I respected the "skip Kidambi-Newton spherical collapse" entry. I did not re-derive anything the ledger marks done and did no identity hunting; I ran only summary-level searches to assess priority for this specific statement. No files were modified in wt-tex or /home/user/GENChase. My working directory, research/priorart-S3-winding-bounds/, is empty because every fetch was blocked.

(a) For a sphere of radius R, (i) reads cos beta = 1 - |ahat|(t_c - t)/R^2; the formula as written is the R = 1 case. The cap-area rate 2 pi |ahat| and the lifetime 2R^2/|ahat| stated in the same result need the /R^2. The stereographic radius is 2R tan(beta/2). (b) In general psi = -(bhat/|ahat|) ln tan(beta/2) + const, where psi is measured right-handed about the outward p. This equals -2 P0 ln tan(beta/2) + const when bhat > 0, which holds for every shape when S > 0, or when psi is measured in the sense of rotation. (c) The extra rotation 2 P0 ln(2/(1+cos beta0)) compares against the planar spiral of the same chord triangle, whose circumradius is R sin beta0. If the planar spiral is instead matched by time to collapse, with planar circumradius |R n_c(0) - p| (the pairing used in (i)), the excess is P0 ln(2/(1+cos beta0)), half as much. 'Every self-similar motion' means every non-rigid one (ahat != 0). bhat != 0 is guaranteed by P > sqrt(3)/2.
result.reasoning:
VERDICT: the result holds. I proved it again by my own route and confirmed it numerically with my own code. The only problems are the three wording issues listed in corrected_statement.

PROOF (my own derivation; it does not use the explorer's scripts or S1's proof)
Setup: Biot-Savart on a sphere of radius R, dx_i/dt = (1/(2 pi R)) sum_j G_j (x_j x x_i)/|x_i - x_j|^2. The vortices lie on the circle x.n = dR, with rho = R sqrt(1 - d^2).

1. Chord lengths. d l_ij^2/dt = (G_m/(pi R)) [x_i,x_j,x_m] (1/l_jm^2 - 1/l_im^2), and [x_i,x_j,x_m] = 2 A_n d R. So the chord dynamics on the sphere are the planar chord dynamics, viewed from the side n points to, multiplied by d.
   - For a planar self-similar shape, dl^2/dt = 2 d (ahat/rho^2) l^2. So the chord ratios are invariant.
   - Then d(rho^2)/dt = 2 d ahat. With rho^2 = R^2(1 - d^2) this gives d' = -ahat/R^2 for d != 0, and by continuity at d = 0.
   - This is (i), with the /R^2.

2. p is fixed. J is conserved. A self-similar motion with changing size forces sum G_i G_j l_ij^2 = 0, which gives |J| = |S|. So p = J/S lies on the sphere, in the plane of the vortices, and hence on the circumcircle. Because p is a fixed affine combination of the vortices, the motion is a similarity about p: v_i = s w_i + Om x w_i, with w_i = x_i - p.

3. Splitting the velocity. x_j x x_i = dR rho n x (e_i - e_j) + rho^2 sin(phi_i - phi_j) n. So the in-plane velocity is d times the planar velocity, which gives s = d ahat/rho^2 and Om.n = d bhat/rho^2.

4. Tangency. From x_i.v_i = 0 and |w|^2 = 2 w.(c - p) on the circle, the in-plane part of Om x p equals s(c - p). Solving gives Om_in.u = bhat/(R rho), and then Om.phat = bhat(d^2/rho^2 + 1/R^2) = bhat/rho^2.

5. The frame (n, u = (p - dRn)/rho, n x u) moves with the similarity and depends only on (beta, psi). So dpsi/dt = Om.phat = bhat/(R^2 sin^2 beta).

6. Integrating: dpsi/dbeta = -(bhat/|ahat|)/sin beta, so psi = -(bhat/|ahat|) ln tan(beta/2) + C, and tan(angle to the meridian) = sin beta |dpsi/dbeta| = 2 P0. That is the loxodrome.
   - The stereographic image from -p is an exact log spiral with d ln r/d psi = -|ahat|/bhat.
   - Both ends of the motion (d -> -1 and d -> +1) shrink the circle to p. The time taken is 2R^2/|ahat|, and the time from beta to collapse is R^2(1 - cos beta)/|ahat|.
   - The chords are stationary at d = 0.
   - The calculus and the extra-rotation limit were checked in sympy (sym_calculus.py).

STATIC CHECK AT 50 DIGITS (static_rates.py; configurations built by my own side-length construction)
- Coverage: 1764 configurations.
  - Circulations: mu = 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 3, plus (-10,-15,6) with S < 0, plus (1,-0.3,3/7).
  - Both orientations; R = 1 and 2.5; beta from 1e-4 to pi - 1e-4, including pi/2; three values of psi.
- Worst relative errors:
  - d(cos beta)/dt vs |ahat|/R^2: 1.3e-42
  - dpsi/dt vs bhat/(R^2 sin^2 beta): 1.6e-42
  - tan(angle to meridian) vs 2 P0: 1.8e-42
  - Om.phat vs psi': 5.8e-43
- Residuals:
  - similarity about p: 1.8e-48
  - |J/S - p|: 6e-51
  - planar self-similarity: 3e-50
  - chord log-rate spread (relative to |ahat|/R^2): 8.5e-39
- In every configuration the sign of dpsi/dt (right-handed about p) equals the sign of bhat.

TRAJECTORY CHECKS
- mpmath.odefun at 40 digits. This is a Taylor method with finite differences at extra precision, a different method from the explorer's AD Taylor integrator. All three runs cross the great circle.
  - mu = 1, from cos beta = -0.86 to 0.99: cos error 7e-40, psi error 6.6e-39 on psi of about 20.
  - mu = 0.2, mirrored orientation, from cos beta = -0.96 to 0.995: cos error 2.2e-39, psi error 3.7e-38 on psi of about 49.
  - mu = 0.05, P0 = 15.9: a partial run to cos beta = -0.17 (the 900 s timeout hit) gave psi error 1.8e-37 on psi of about 50.
  - Chord-ratio drift is at most 1.7e-39, and |J/S - p| is at most 2.5e-41.
- scipy DOP853 in double precision (rtol 1e-13), full lifetime run forward and backward to rho/R = 1.4e-3, six cases including R = 2.5 and R = 0.7, S < 0, and mu = 0.05.
  - cos beta law: error at most 2.6e-11.
  - psi law: error at most 1.2e-7 relative, over total rotations of 30 to 78 rad.
  - Both ends converge to the same p (max |x_i - p|/R = 2.8e-3 at beta = 1.4e-3 and at pi - 1.4e-3). So the burst is from p, not from 'some other point'.
  - The integrated span matches 2R^2/|ahat| to 10 digits.
- Shape survey on a 199x199 grid (sign_bhat.py): bhat > 0 for every L = 0 shape, both orientations, mu = 0.01 to 4 (S > 0). The grid minimum of P0 reproduces sqrt(2) at mu = 1 and 1.0647 at mu = 1/2.

CAVEATS (none changes the mathematics)
(a) Part (i) as written omits /R^2. The statement is only internally consistent for R = 1.
(b) The sign of psi is a convention. As written it is right-handed about outward p when S > 0; for S < 0 the rotation reverses.
(c) The 'extra rotation' depends on how the planar spiral is matched.
   - Same chord triangle (circumradius R sin beta0): 2 P0 ln(2/(1+cos beta0)), as claimed.
   - Same time to collapse: P0 ln(2/(1+cos beta0)), exactly half (checked in sympy at several beta0).
(d) Rigid relative equilibria (ahat = 0) are excluded.

NOVELTY: not assessed independently; I did not search. The explorer's prior-art note (Borisov-Lebedev 1998, Kidambi-Newton) is consistent with the RESEARCH.md ledger.

No source I found states a minimum, or any bound, on the rotation of four-vortex collapse over all circulations and shapes. That covers P, Omega*tau, B/(-2A), the spiral angle, the angle per e-fold and the normalized path length. Two directly relevant papers are still unread.

Closest risks:
1. O'Neil, "Relative equilibrium and collapse configurations of four point vortices", Regul. Chaotic Dyn. 12 (2007) 117-126.
   - How I know: WebSearch abstract only. The Springer body is blocked. This is not the Physica D 236 triple-ring paper the repo already read.
   - What it does: for fixed circulations, it gives a computational method that "yields all configurations with a given ratio of velocity to position" (that ratio is kappa, so its argument is P). It does not prove finiteness for collapse.
   - Why it matters: it could show the kappa range for example circulations. The abstract gives no sign of optimizing over circulations. This is the main unread risk.
2. Kallyadan and Shukla, Phys. Rev. Fluids 7, 114701 (2022).
   - How I know: abstract only. The APS body is blocked, and the ledger records it as numerical families.
   - What it does: one-parameter families of collapse and expansion configurations for given circulations, passing through finitely many rigid configurations.
   - Why it matters: plots of kappa along a family could show a minimum of P for particular circulations. A global minimum over circulations is not suggested.
3. Xiang Yu, arXiv:2103.06037 and arXiv:2111.07292. Hampton and Moeckel, Trans. AMS 361 (2009).
   - How I know: search summaries only.

result.reasoning:
Why I think the result is probably not in the literature:
- To state it, a paper would have to minimize arg(kappa) over the whole three-dimensional set of normalized four-vortex collapses, across circulations as well as shapes.
- The four-vortex literature I could reach does something else. It proves finiteness (O'Neil 2007, Hampton-Moeckel 2009, Yu 2021-22), finds configurations by root-finding or residual minimization (Lewkowicz, Kudela, Kallyadan-Shukla), or gives symmetric closed families (Novikov-Sedov, Koiller, Gotoda, Demina-Kudryashov).
- The spiral coefficient Im/(2 Re) does appear as a formula (Aref 2010 eq. 29c; Kudela 2021 eq. 14), but nobody optimizes it.
- The simpler three-vortex bound P > sqrt(3)/2 was not found in the literature despite this project's extensive search. That makes a four-vortex global optimum being in print less likely still.

Residual risk (conservatively 10-15 per cent for some equivalent statement):
- O'Neil's RCD 2007 paper parametrizes four-vortex collapse configurations by exactly the ratio kappa, and Kallyadan-Shukla trace kappa along families. Either might show a local minimum of P for particular circulations, or an example with a spiral angle below 60 degrees. That would partly anticipate the "below the three-vortex floor" remark, though not the global value P_4.
- Read both before any claim, and say that O'Neil's method is the natural tool for checking the result.

Side finding, a conflict to resolve before writing this up:

VERDICT: the identity is correct. I re-derived the proof by hand and checked it with my own code at 50 to 60 digits. The one gap: the P formula writes sigma without an absolute value, and sigma >= 0 is unproved. It is numerically supported everywhere I looked, including every collapse configuration found.

PROOF CHECK (by hand, all steps confirmed)
- From the Biot-Savart law: conj(kappa) conj(w_j) = (1/2 pi i) sum_k G_k/(w_j - w_k). Multiply by 2 pi i w_j and use w_j/(w_j - w_k) = (1 + K_jk)/2 with K = D + iE. This gives 4 pi i conj(kappa) s = Gt 1 - (I - K) G.
- Real part: (I - D) G = Gt 1 - 4 pi Im(kappa) s. Imaginary part: E G = 4 pi Re(kappa) s.
- Formula check: D_jk = (s_j - s_k)/|w_j - w_k|^2 and E_jk = 2 Im(conj(w_j) w_k)/|w_j - w_k|^2, both antisymmetric.
- Because D is antisymmetric, x^T (I + D) x = |x|^2. So I + D is invertible, v^T s = |v|^2 > 0 (s is nonzero unless all vortices sit at one point), and v^T (I - D) G = ((I + D) v)^T G = s^T G = L. Projecting both equations onto v gives the two formulas.
- A vortex exactly at z_c gives D_jk = -1 and E_jk = 0 in its row. Its row equation then holds trivially, as claimed.
- The G-weighted sum uses G^T K G = 0 (K is antisymmetric). It gives sum_{i<j} G_i G_j = 2 pi (Im kappa + i Re kappa) L. So Re(kappa) != 0 forces L = 0 and sum_{i<j} G_i G_j = 0.
- The corollaries follow: Im kappa = Gt sigma/(4 pi |v|^2), Re kappa = v^T E G/(4 pi |v|^2), and "no rotation iff sigma = 0" because Gt != 0 and |v|^2 > 0.
- P = |Im kappa|/(-2 Re kappa) = |Gt| |sigma| / (2 |v^T E G|). The statement drops the absolute value on sigma. That is only valid if sigma >= 0, which the proof does not show.

The ratios lie between 1.33 and 8.1 and are consistent with half the eigenvalues. The point is a strict local minimum.

3. Global search, float64 (nv.py, global_search.py). I used a symmetric formulation with all four E_j and a generic rotation gauge. There were 12,000 random starts, with circulations drawn from [-g, g] for g = 0.3, 1, 2 and 3, followed by SLSQP minimization of b^2.
- 3,407 runs converged. 3,404 of them end at P = 0.7978968.
- The other 3 are not KKT points: the stationarity residual is 0.15 to 0.87 and P is 0.813 or higher, so SLSQP stopped early.
- Across all 3,488 feasible endpoints, including runs that did not converge, the minimum is P_4 up to 2.5e-13 of float roundoff.

- One circulation goes to 0 with the others O(1): the limit is a three-vortex collapse, and P > sqrt(3)/2 is proved in the paper.
- Two O(1) circulations and two weak ones: the strong pair only co-rotates, so Re kappa -> 0 and P -> infinity.
- An O(1)-strength cluster cannot shrink, because its velocities would be unbounded.
- The remaining degeneration is a strong vortex plus a weak cluster of strength eps and size about eps.

  - Three facts hold: the virial identity makes the cluster translate with V = -i sigma/(2 pi conj(D)), using sigma = -S2 from sum GiGj = 0; the strain of the strong vortex gives dD/dt = -sigma V + U_zbar conj(D); and self-similarity requires kappa C = U(C) + V and kappa D = dD/dt.

- This argument is asymptotic and heuristic, not rigorous, so the 'is a minimum' part remains numerical evidence, as the explorer labeled it.

result.reasoning:
WHAT IS STANDARD
The result has three layers, and they carry different risk.

- The starting equation is textbook. It says sum_k Gamma_k w_j/(w_j - w_k) = 2 pi i conj(kappa) s_j, which is the result's equation 4 pi i conj(kappa) s = Gamma_tot 1 - (I-K)Gamma. It is O'Neil 2007 eq. (2.3) in ring form, Demina-Kudryashov eq. (11), Gotoda (2.4) and Kudela (10).
- The Gamma-weighted sum is classical: it gives sum GiGj = 2 pi(Im kappa + i Re kappa)L, and hence L = 0 and sum GiGj = 0 for any collapse. See Novikov-Sedov 1979, O'Neil 2007 eq. (2.5) and Demina-Kudryashov eqs. (26)-(28).
- Splitting (w_j + w_k)/(w_j - w_k) into real antisymmetric parts D and E and using linearity in Gamma is very likely implicit in Kallyadan-Shukla 2022. Its abstract says it treats self-similarity as a linear system at fixed shape. I could not read it.

WHAT I DID NOT FIND
The part that does the work is the choice of test vector v = (I+D)^{-1}s. Because (I+D)^T = I-D, it satisfies v^T(I-D)Gamma = s^T Gamma = L. That collapses the dependence on the circulations to Gamma_tot and L, and leaves one scalar, sigma(w) = 1^T(I+D)^{-1}s, which depends only on the shape and controls the sign of the rotation.

No source I read has this, or any other formula for Im kappa whose numerator depends on Gamma only through Gamma_tot and L:
- Gotoda's Prop. 2.1 is a per-pair formula that involves every Gamma_l.
- The obvious unweighted projection gives Im kappa = ((N-1)Gamma_tot + 1^T D Gamma)/(4 pi sum s). That still involves Gamma through D.
- O'Neil 2007 and Demina-Kudryashov 2014 have only the weighted identity.

THE COROLLARY
"Non-rotating collapse exists iff some collapsing configuration has sigma = 0" follows directly from the identity. The question behind it is visible in the literature but I found no answer:
- Demina-Kudryashov note that beta = 0 would mean collapse along fixed rays.
- O'Neil 2007 Prop. 6 excludes Re omega = 0.
- Kudela's definition requires lambda_i != 0.
- Yu's four-vortex finiteness analysis, known only from summaries, singles out Lambda = +/-i (probably the non-rotating case; my inference) with Novikov-Sedov-type circulations.
None of these gives a geometric criterion like sigma.

WHY "UNCLEAR" RATHER THAN "PROBABLY UNSTATED"
The algebra is elementary, one screen of linear algebra. The general-N literature on stationary configurations is large, algebraic and mostly unread here. O'Neil 1987 (Trans. AMS, 43 pages), Kallyadan-Shukla 2022, Yu 2021 I/II, Lewkowicz 2015, Kudela 2014 and Newton's 2001 book were all blocked or seen only as summaries, and each could contain an equivalent projection or a sign-of-rotation lemma. The closest risk is Kallyadan-Shukla. Summaries are weak evidence of absence.

SANITY CHECK
Script: research/priorart-kappa-identity/indep_check.py, my own code, run at 50 digits. On the (1, 1, -1/2) three-vortex circle, collapsing and expanding points, direct Biot-Savart kappa matches the formula to about 1e-50. The same holds for three configurations each from the N = 5, 6 and 8 files produced by check-kappa-identity. In every case sigma > 0 and L is about 1e-51.

TWO THINGS FOR THE STATEMENT
1. Wording. "P = |Gamma_tot| sigma/(2|v^T E Gamma|)" should read |Gamma_tot||sigma|, unless sigma >= 0 is proved. The statement itself treats sigma = 0 as open, and P is defined with |Im kappa|.
2. Novelty language. Say the formula "was not found in O'Neil 2007, Demina-Kudryashov 2014, Gotoda 2021 or Kudela 2021". Say that O'Neil 1987, Kallyadan-Shukla 2022 and Yu 2021 were not checked. Do not claim novelty and do not attach a name.

For all of these, the self-similarity residual measured by direct Biot-Savart is 1e-30 to 1e-61, the sum of Gamma_i Gamma_j and the angular impulse L vanish to the same level, Re kappa < 0, no circulation is near zero (min|G|/max|G| >= 0.057) and no two vortices are near each other (min distance / radius >= 0.05).

2. Strict local minima. I computed the Hessian of the Lagrangian, restricted to the tangent space, by finite differences of the analytic gradient in mpmath. It is positive definite for N=5 to 13, 21, 29 and 31. The smallest eigenvalues are 1.287, 1.029, 0.872, 0.766, 0.0290, 0.0153, 0.0101, 0.00564, 0.00424, 3.78e-4, 8.30e-5 and 6.14e-5. The explorer's values are in a different gauge, so only the signs compare. As a cross-check at N=5 and N=9, I moved along six random tangent directions and projected back onto the manifold. P^2 rises on both sides every time, and the second derivatives fall within the eigenvalue range.

3. Global search, my own method. Random Gamma and z, then least squares to feasibility, then SLSQP, then Newton polishing and the Hessian test.
- N=5: 3000 starts gave 162 KKT points, all at 0.744814456962. It is the only local minimum found.
- N=6: 1500 starts gave 90 KKT points: 0.713680 (43 times) and 0.802268 (47).
- N=7: 2000 starts gave 90: 0.693662 (11), 0.734465 (52) and 0.756334 (27).
- N=8: 1500 starts gave 38: 0.679770 (2), 0.694411 (31) and 0.728709 (5).
- N=9: 1500 starts gave 15: 0.659260 (7, two-armed), 0.669581 (one-armed) and 0.669879.
- N=10: 1000 starts gave 2 KKT points, both at 0.637706.

Nothing below the claimed values was found. SLSQP runs that failed ended infeasible, with residual about 1, not at low-P configurations. The evidence is weak at N=8 to 10, where few starts converged.

4. Structure is confirmed. For N=5 to 8 there is one negative vortex and a strong positive vortex near z_c (|z|/R = 0.06 to 0.08). The weak positive vortices form a chain (principal-component aspect ratio 0.09 to 0.12), with the negative vortex near the outer end. For odd N >= 9 there is a central Gamma_max vortex at z_c, two equal negative vortices, and a nearly straight chain (aspect ratio 0.046). The configuration maps to itself under z -> -z to 1e-16. At N=9 the one-armed minimum 0.66958 is above the two-armed 0.65926, and at N=8 the two-armed 0.69441 is above the one-armed 0.67977. For even N see correction (4).

5. Extrapolation, tested independently. I grew the two-arm family with my own insertion of a symmetric pair into the largest gap, followed by descent. Starting from N=13 it reproduced the explorer's N=15, 17, 19 and 21 to 15 digits. I then continued from N=31 to N=89. Every step is a strict local minimum, symmetric to 1e-12, with residual 1e-14. Fits to the explorer's N <= 31 data predicted N=41, 51 and 81 to within 2e-6, 5e-6 and 2e-5, with the computed values slightly lower each time. On the N <= 81 data, polynomial fits in 1/m, power-law fits (exponent 0.996 to 0.997) and fits with a log term all give 0.47734 to 0.47744, and they predict N=83 to 89 to 1e-10. So the limit is about 0.4774, just below the explorer's quoted fit range.

The one-armed fits give 0.6014 to 0.6063 depending on the model (0.6037 for polynomials). The three-armed branch refits to 0.553. The four-armed branch refits to 0.615 to 0.622, with an odd/even alternation in m. I rebuilt the full symmetric configurations and they reproduce the explorer's P values.

6. Further checks.
- N=33 and N=61 were certified by high-precision projection onto the manifold: P = 0.517229132219544023 (residual 1e-40) and P = 0.498184439159713880 (residual 5.5e-30).
- Integrating the equations of motion (DOP853) from N=5, 9 and 21 matches the self-similar prediction to 1e-12 to 1e-14 at t = 0.5 t_c. Deviations then grow, and they scale with injected perturbations of 1e-12 to 1e-8, so they are a linear dynamical instability of these collapses, not an error in the configurations. The claim does not address stability.
- Novelty was not assessed.

I checked this independently with my own code, without running the explorer's scripts. My scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-GENChase/04604b4b-7efe-5ca6-9b53-4838030930e5/scratchpad/research/check-A4/ (bs.py, sym_proof.py, corner.py, scan.py, chainfail2.py, values.py, ode.py, extra.py).

1. Formula for P, derived by hand. The velocity is dz_j/dt = i sum_k G_k (z_j - z_k) |z_j - z_k|^(-2beta), with beta = 1 + alpha/2. This gives d(r_i^2)/dt = ±4 A G_i (f_j - f_k), with f = r^(-2beta). Self-similarity means the three quantities G_i (f_j - f_k)/r_i^2 share one value c. So on any scalene triangle the circulations are fixed up to scale and are real. Isosceles and equilateral shapes force c = 0, so they do not collapse; collinear shapes do not collapse either. Working out Im kappa gives Im kappa = c S/2 and Re kappa = ±2Ac, where S = sum over cyclic (i,j,k) of r_i^2 (f_j + f_k)/(f_j - f_k). Hence P = |S|/(8A). |S| is symmetric under permutations of the sides because a transposition only flips its sign, so ordering the sides is allowed. The explorer's S agrees with this; note coth b = (Y+1)/(Y-1).

2. Biot-Savart check. I found the circulations separately, as the null vector of the complex condition (v2 - v1)(z3 - z1) = (v3 - v1)(z2 - z1), not from the formula. On 4200 random scalene triangles, over 14 values of alpha from -0.89 to 30, at 50 digits:
- P agrees with |S|/(8A) to within 4e-48 (relative).
- The self-similarity residual over all three vortices is at most 1e-49.
- Re kappa < 0 in every case once the mirror image is taken where needed. The mirror sends kappa to -conj(kappa), so either a shape or its mirror collapses.
- P - B > 0 in every case.

3. The proof, step by step, all confirmed.
- SymPy confirms g'(x) = x^3(24 - x)/((12 + 6x - x^2)^2 (1 + x)) exactly. The root of 12 + 6x - x^2 is 3 + sqrt21, and the series of 1/ln(1+x) starts 1/x + 1/2 - x/12.
- The identity in step (iii) holds exactly (SymPy residual 0).
- Case m < 2: the bracket exceeds 2beta - 1, since beta m^2 < 4beta and rho m < 2.
- Case m >= 2: I rechecked the bound -(2+3beta)/3 myself. With h(rho) = rho^2 (1 + 6beta - beta(2+rho)^2 - rho(2+rho)), I get h(1) = -3beta - 2, and h(rho) - h(1) factors as (1 - rho) times a positive polynomial. The square is > 4beta^2 because 1 + 2beta - rho > 2beta. The root of 12beta^2 - 3beta - 2 is 0.5519563, so the alpha threshold is -0.8960874 and the stated alpha > -0.896 is covered.
- Step (i) holds because (t+X)/(t-X) decreases for t > X, and Y > 1 > X.
- Lam > 0 holds because rho^2 m/6 < rho/2.
- The chain is sound, and it also shows S > 0, so |S| = S.

4. Sharpness. As rho -> 0 we have X/rho -> 0 (because beta > 1/2), so S/rho -> m + 2/(beta m). Then P -> (beta m^2 + 2)/(2 beta m sqrt(4 - m^2)). SymPy finds the single critical point m* = sqrt(2/(1+beta)), where the value equals B exactly.
- At 60 digits, for alpha in {-0.89, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 10}, P - B goes to 0 from above. It shrinks like rho^2 for alpha >= 0 and like rho^(2beta) for alpha < 0.
- At rho = 1e-6 and m = m*, the Biot-Savart value is P - B = 1.76e-13, 1.65e-13, 1.59e-13, 1.57e-13 for alpha = 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, with residual below 1e-60. This matches the explorer's 1.6e-13.
- At rho = 1e-6 the circulations are about (1e-6, 1, -1e-6) at alpha = 0, and G1/G2 is of order rho^(2beta-1). So two weak, opposite vortices form a dipole beside a strong one, as stated.
- cos psi -> -m*/2, so the dipole axis, taken as an undirected line, makes the angle arccos(1/sqrt(2(1+beta))) with the line to the strong vortex.

5. Global scans.
- Grid: about 220 values of rho (from 1e-10 to 1 - 1e-10, clustered at both ends), times about 125 values of m clustered at both edges, for 25 values of alpha from -0.8959 to 100, at 35 digits. S > 0 everywhere, P > B everywhere, and the smallest values occur toward rho -> 0 with m near m*.
- About 4350 grid points flagged failures of the chain at 35 digits. All of them were precision artifacts: every one passes at 120 digits, and the smallest relative gap was 4.5e-41.
- A random stress test at 120 digits (20000 points each for alpha = -0.896, -0.89, 0, 1, 1000) found no violation of the chain.

6. Dynamical claims, checked by integrating the ODE (DOP853, rtol 1e-13) up to t_c(1 - 1e-9) for alpha = -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2.
- Deriving it myself: |g|^(2beta) = 1 + 2beta Re(kappa0) t, so t_c = -1/(2beta Re kappa0) and |omega_0| t_c = P/beta = 2P/(2+alpha). The integrated scale factor matches this to within 6e-6 relative at alpha = 1, 0.5 and 2 (1e-5 at alpha = 0, 7e-3 at alpha = -0.5, where the shape drifts by 6e-3 near the end).
- The rotation angle equals (Im kappa/Re kappa) ln s to within 4e-6 relative at alpha = 1, 0.5 and 2 (3e-4 at alpha = -0.5).
- Path lengths equal r0 sqrt(1+4P^2)(1 - s) to within 1e-6, which is the precision the output was printed at.
- So the path-ratio bound (4+alpha)/(2+alpha), the spiral-angle bound arccos((2+alpha)/(4+alpha)) and the bound on |omega_0| t_c all follow.
- Every tabulated value checks at 40 digits: P_min, the path ratios 2, 9/5, 5/3, 11/7, 3/2, and the angles 60, 56.25, 53.13, 50.48, 48.19 degrees.
- B(alpha) is decreasing because its derivative has the sign of -(4 + alpha); it tends to 0 and equals sqrt3/2 at alpha = 0.

Caveats that do not affect the statement:
- "P_min" is an infimum, not a minimum; the statement itself says it is not attained.
- The theorem covers self-similar collapse only. The ledger records that SQG also has non-self-similar collapse.
- The limit -0.896 comes from the proof method. A coarse grid at alpha = -0.95, -0.99, -1.2, -1.5 still shows P > B, but that range is not claimed and I did not check it further.
- I did not verify the explorer's supporting claim that the minimum over psi at fixed rho is unique and increases with rho. The theorem does not depend on it.
- Novelty is outside this check. The ledger's gSQG rows, including the one for arXiv:2505.19782, record no such bound, and the literature caveats in the explorer's note stand.

result.reasoning:
No source I could reach states the result in any equivalent form. That covers:
- a minimum of |Im kappa|/(-2 Re kappa), Omega tau, B/(-2A), the spiral pitch or angle, or the normalized path length, taken over N-vortex self-similar collapses at fixed N;
- how such a minimum depends on N;
- the one-arm/two-arm structure of the minimizers;
- any extrapolated limit or bound on the infimum over N.
The same quantity is not minimized in the literature even for N = 3; only this project's own paper does that. The N-vortex papers (Kudela 2014/2021, Lewkowicz-Kudela, Gotoda 2021, Kallyadan-Shukla, Demina-Kudryashov) compute configurations and report collapse time and Hamiltonian, sometimes the spiral law. None of them optimizes the spin-to-collapse ratio.

Caveats that should shape the wording:
(a) The configuration class is published. Kudela 2021 showed numerically that when a few strong vortices are present, the weak ones gather on sheets. His two-strong-vortex case A1 (two strong negative vortices and a chain of 48 unit positive vortices, antisymmetric and sinusoidal-like, straightening to a nearly straight line) closely resembles the two-arm minimizers. O'Neil 2010 found collapsing vortex sheets, approximated by point vortices, which is the natural N -> infinity limit. Any write-up should cite both as precursors and claim only the P-minimality and the numbers.
(b) Explicit published configurations already have P below sqrt3/2 without saying so. The Demina-Kudryashov 2014 Table 1 seven-vortex example gives P = 0.805357, recomputed here by Biot-Savart. That is consistent with the claimed N = 7 minimum of 0.6937.
(c) "Smallest known P" should read "smallest P found here". Kudela's N = 50 configurations and O'Neil's sheet collapses have P values that were never computed; they are not prior art for the result, but they could in principle sit below the reported values. I tried to evaluate P on Kudela's published circulation sets: 49 x (+1) with one -24, and 48 x (+1) with two vortices a = -48 +/- sqrt1176. I used an independent fixed-circulation Levenberg-Marquardt solver (research/priorart-R5-nvortex/kudela_fixedG.py). In float64 it did not converge from random starts within the 5-minute budget (residual about 3.9 after 200 iterations), so the check is inconclusive. Kudela reports needing 500-digit arithmetic for his method.
(d) The main unread risk is O'Neil 2010: if it tabulates rotation and collapse rates for sheet collapses, it would nearly contain the limiting claim.

As a sanity check, not a novelty argument, I re-evaluated four certified configurations by direct Biot-Savart at 50 digits (research/priorart-R5-nvortex/bs_check.py): n5_cert60, n6_cert60, k2cert_21 and k2cert_29.
- P agrees with the claimed values to at least 28 digits: 0.744814456962492461..., 0.713680148529392474..., 0.542907185837218003... and 0.523220743518951920....
- The self-similarity spread is 1e-39 for N = 5 and 6, 3e-26 for N = 21 and 5e-22 for N = 29. These floors come from the precision of the stored strings.
- Re kappa < 0 in all four, and L and sum GiGj are about 0.

The rating is "probably unstated" rather than "unclear" because none of the read texts or summaries contains even the concept of minimizing P over configurations. It is not stronger than that because three relevant bodies (O'Neil 2010, Kudela 2014 JNS/FDR, Kallyadan-Shukla) are unread, arXiv is blocked, and search summaries are weak evidence.

Suggested ledger line, to be added by whoever may write to the repo: "2026-09-24 R5 N-vortex min P: Kudela Energies 2021 read in full (sheets with strong vortices; only Tc and H; no P); DK2014 Table 1 has an implicit P = 0.8054 at N = 7; O'Neil TCFD 2010, Kudela JNS/FDR 2014 and Kallyadan-Shukla 2022 unread; no source minimizes P over N-vortex collapses."
